authors: Albertazzi, U.; Djekic, D.; Ponte Marques, A.
title: Physical climate risk, credit risk and lending activity
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (Sections 1-3, 5.3, Table 17, opening of 6)
question: Causal effect of floods on lending, rates, collateral requirements and default of pre-existing loans
data: AnaCredit loans >=EUR 25,000 located by borrower registered address + Copernicus EMS maps; four floods 2021-2024; ECB 0-5 hazard indicator (RCP 4.5)
identification: Spatial RD at flood boundary (local linear, triangular kernel, CCT bandwidths ~360-460 m); firm-time FE for supply vs demand
main_finding: Default ratio +0.568 pp after one quarter (10% level; Table 8, p. 27) and +0.64-0.69 pp over two quarters (Table 9, p. 28), ~doubling a 1.4% annual rate; 0.4-0.9 pp across bandwidths. Real-estate-backed micro-firm loans: LTV +5.3 pp, large-firm interaction -6.2 pp (Table 17, p. 39)
how_my_project_differs: Borrower address not collateral location; no LGD or staging; insured/aided advanced economies; project adds collateral-level exposure, LGD, staging and relief censoring

authors: Blickle, K. S.; Hamerling, S. N.; Morgan, D. P.
title: How Bad Are Weather Disasters for Banks?
venue: Federal Reserve Bank of New York Staff Report 990 (Nov 2021, rev. Oct 2025); published version J. Money, Credit and Banking 2026, doi 10.1111/jmcb.70036
question: How much weather disasters hurt bank performance and stability, and why
data: FEMA disasters 1995-2018; SHELDUS county damage; branch-based exposure; FEMA flood maps + HMDA
identification: Panel with saturated FE; non-FEMA vs FEMA disasters and state-border discontinuities for aid
main_finding: Effects small; local banks hit more but a disaster 6.7 SD beyond the 95th percentile would be needed to push a single-county bank to failure; loan demand and local knowledge (avoiding tracts where FEMA maps understate risk) mitigate
how_my_project_differs: Loan/collateral-level rather than bank-level; provisioning and capital via ECL; reverse stress test in a setting without FEMA-style aid or broad insurance

authors: Caloia, F.; Jansen, D.-J.
title: Flood risk and financial stability: Evidence from a stress test for the Netherlands
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (Sections 1 and 5)
question: How much would floods of increasing severity deplete Dutch banks' capital?
data: Geocoded real-estate collateral of ten banks (>95% of sector assets) matched to flood inundation scenarios
identification: Scenario stress test with PD/LGD modules; six scenarios (1, 3, 5 m; unprotected vs protected areas); self-described as 'in essence' a reverse stress test
main_finding: CET1 -110 bp (1 m) to -132 bp (5 m) in unprotected areas (p. 22); protected west -307 bp (1 m), ~-400 bp (3 m), -712 bp (5 m) (p. 23); residential damage contributes 402 bp in the extreme case via LGD and RWA (p. 24)
how_my_project_differs: Modelled hazard, scenario escalation rather than formal inversion; insured, protected advanced economy; project estimates elasticities from realised floods and solves for the breaking severity under relief

authors: Chitchumnong, P.; Hatairatana, A.; Khangphukhieo, W.
title: Physical Climate Risk Stress Test: An Evidence-based Approach
venue: CRC Working Papers, Credit Research Centre, University of Edinburgh
question: What was the impact of the 2011 Thai flood on a bank's mortgage default, and how can it feed a physical climate stress test?
data: Proprietary Thai bank mortgage portfolio 2009-2013; Royal Irrigation Department runoff at Nakhon Sawan since 1979
identification: Vintage (age-period-cohort) default model: benchmark plus macro variables (lower bound); flood-affected vs unaffected borrower lifecycles (upper bound); extreme value analysis for scenario probability
main_finding: Modest mortgage default impact, dampened by debt relief and rapid recovery; flood-affected borrowers riskier; auto-loan defaults spiked; 2011 runoff about 1-in-50-year event
how_my_project_differs: Collateral-level satellite exposure; LGD and IFRS 9 staging rather than default rates only; relief modelled as treatment; formal reverse stress test; multi-bank or public-data design

authors: Dhima, J.; Iravani, M.A.; Itam, E.; Boidot, T.
title: Integration of physical climate risks into banks' credit risk and capital assessment: a case study on the impact of flooding on real estate portfolios

identification: Extended Merton (1974) structural model with flood damage to collateral
main_finding: Flooding affects PD, LGD and capital, but not systematically when damage is below expected return on immovable assets; material for already-vulnerable firms
how_my_project_differs: Empirical estimation with observed floods and Thai collateral; adds IFRS 9 staging and reverse stress test

authors: Dolk, M.; Dunz, N.; Lesage, F.; Nie, O.; Pollitt, H.

authors: European Central Bank

authors: Gallagher, J.; Hartley, D.
title: Household Finance after a Natural Disaster: The Case of Hurricane Katrina

authors: Garbarino, N.; Guin, B.
title: High water, no marks? Biased lending after extreme weather

authors: Giné, Xavier; Kanz, Martin
title: The Economic Effects of a Borrower Bailout: Evidence from an Emerging Market
question: Credit-market and real effects of India's 2008 farm-loan waiver
data: RBI district and bank-district credit data; regional productivity, wage and employment data
identification: District exposure from retrospective land-pledge eligibility rule; bank-district FE for local demand
main_finding: 1 s.d. more exposure: loans -4-6%, credit -13-16%; credit reallocated away from high-exposure districts; loan performance worsens among previously good borrowers; precise zero real effects; defaults track the electoral cycle
how_my_project_differs: Shows relief-induced moral hazard in an EM; the project asks whether flood relief similarly masks and defers PD/LGD effects and what that means for ECL

authors: Mukherjee, Saptarshi; Subramanian, Krishnamurthy; Tantri, Prasanna

authors: Noy, I.; Nguyen, C.; Patel, P.
title: Floods and Spillovers: Households after the 2011 Great Flood in Thailand
venue: Economic Development and Cultural Change 69(2):829-868 (CESifo WP 7644)
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (WP version: data, Section 5 text, conclusions; tables not read)

main_finding: Business income falls THB 6,465 (direct) and THB 4,018 (spillover) (Section 5.3, p. 26); total spending unchanged, housing up, luxuries down; longer floods roughly double income effects; debt and savings effects small and insignificant (unreported; pp. 22-23)

authors: Pérez Montes, C.; García Villasur, J.; Gutiérrez de Rozas, L.; Jiménez, G.; Lavín, N.; Matyunina, A.; Vegas, R.
title: The impact of the autumn 2024 flash floods in Spain from a financial stability standpoint
venue: Banco de España Financial Stability Review 48, pp. 5-40
verified: 2026-11-02 via Banco de España PDF + Crossref
question: Size and quality of bank exposures in areas hit by the Oct 2024 Valencia floods; did credit, stage 2 and stage 3 diverge afterwards?
data: Copernicus flood geolocation + Central Credit Register (CIRBE) + Cadastre (geolocated real-estate collateral); Sep 2024-Feb 2025
identification: Borrower-level DiD; treatment = postcodes of RDL 6/2024 municipalities (borrower or collateral); PSM control from Mediterranean-coast postcodes; firm/household, sector x time and main-bank x time FE
main_finding: Firms: stage 2 share +~0.5 pp Dec 2024-Jan 2025 (+4.5% rel.), NPL +3.4% rel. from Jan 2025 (pp. 19-20). Households: stage 2 +0.45 pp in Dec only (+4.1%), stage 3 +0.44 pp (+9.1%) (p. 21). Banks with >40% of credit in affected areas: stage 2 to affected firms +24%, stage 3 -9% (p. 21). Authors note moratoria may have flattered credit quality (p. 17).
how_my_project_differs: First evidence that floods surface in stage 2 and that exposed banks shift stage 3 into stage 2 under relief (H-S5a); project adds an emerging market with thin insurance, national-scale event, satellite intensity, LGD and collateral values, multi-year horizon

authors: Sastry
title: Who Bears Flood Risk? Evidence from Mortgage Markets in Florida
question: Do mortgage lenders screen for uninsurable flood risk?
data: Florida mortgage market data (details beyond abstract not read)
identification: Strict NFIP coverage limits plus staggered flood-map updates
main_finding: Lenders require lower LTVs at origination for uninsurable flood risk; delinquency rates equalise inside and outside flood zones; borrower composition shifts to richer, higher-credit-quality households.
how_my_project_differs: Shows lenders respond through LTV when residual risk is retained. In Thailand most flood risk is uninsured, so my project tests whether LTV, appraisal haircuts or provisioning carry that response.

authors: Sawada, Nakata, Sekiguchi, Okuyama
title: Land and Real Estate Price Sensitivity to a Disaster: Evidence from the 2011 Thai Floods
question: Did the 2011 Thai floods lower land and real estate prices?
data: JETRO survey land prices for about 40 industrial estates (10 rounds, Oct 2008-Nov 2012); Agency for Real Estate Affairs (AREA) price series for 43 districts in 9 provinces, 2010-2013, by land use and dwelling type
identification: DiD: seven flooded industrial estates vs others (estate FE, pre-trend test); flooded provinces (Ayutthaya, Pathum Thani, Nonthaburi) vs non-flooded provinces (district FE)
main_finding: Industrial land prices fell (8.27% of mean post-flood, JETRO; 6.49% AREA); townhouse prices fell 4.85%; residential and commercial land, detached houses and condominiums showed no significant change. Authors read this as illiquidity or other frictions.
how_my_project_differs: Province-level treatment and district price series only; no hazard (ex-ante) measure, no satellite exposure, no official Treasury appraisal values, no lender valuations. My project moves to parcel/collateral-level exposure and to appraisal and credit outcomes.

authors: Shala, I.; Schumacher, B.
title: The impact of natural disasters on banks' impairment flow - Evidence from Germany

main_finding: Higher but ephemeral impairment flow, driven by corporate (agriculture, manufacturing) and some mortgage loans; authors conclude expected-loss provisioning was insufficient
how_my_project_differs: Loan-level collateral exposure and IFRS 9 staging; thin-insurance emerging market with debt relief

authors: Tellman, B.; Sullivan, J.A.; Kuhn, C.; Kettner, A.J.; Doyle, C.S.; Brakenridge, G.R.; Erickson, T.A.; Slayback, D.A.; et al.

authors: Van Gerwen, Degryse, Ongena, Scopelliti
title: Flooded Collateral: Bank Asset Management and Lending Decisions
question: Do banks incorporate flood risk into collateral valuations and lending decisions?
data: Loan and collateral data from one major Belgian bank matched to Flemish government flood-risk maps
identification: 2021 Western European floods as a salience shock (pre/post by exposure of collateral)
main_finding: After the floods, collateral exposed to pluvial or sea-level-rise risk is revalued downward; internal staff account for these risks more than external experts and the bank shifts to internal models; rates rise on floating-rate loans of exposed firms but exposure is not cut.
how_my_project_differs: One bank in a rich country, corporate collateral. My project targets an emerging market and links exposure to PD, LGD and ECL staging rather than valuation alone; the title overlap with 'Underwater Collateral' should be acknowledged.

Table 21 lists relief measures; SFIs front ~THB 183 bn (p.69)

main_finding: 6.4 bp average premium in high-risk areas, larger for longer loans, smaller borrowers and local specialised banks; none for firms with intangible/movable assets; flooded-county firms default more Default dynamics (Table 7): 90-day default hazard ratio 0.93 within 6 months of a county flood, 1.20 within 12 and 1.61 within 24 (cumulative windows); authors conjecture emergency aid and payment suspensions, without relief data; bank-reported LGD unresponsive (App. C).
how_my_project_differs: Pricing and PD in Europe; I add collateral LGD, ECL staging and EM debt relief

authors: Beltran, Maddison, Elliott

main_finding: Estimates range from -75.5% to +61.0%; coastal floodplain estimates positive, likely due to omitted amenities, with publication bias; time since last flood matters; inland 100-year floodplain discount of -4.6% as a rule of thumb.
how_my_project_differs: Benchmark for magnitudes; my project would add an emerging-market, appraisal-based estimate; the abstract does not say whether the meta-sample contains any.

title: Rising Waters, Falling Taxes: The Impact of Hurricane Sandy on Property Tax Assessments in New York City
venue: Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 138:103313 (June 2026); read as working paper of 23 June 2025, PDF hosted at brookings.edu
verified: 2026-11-02 via Crossref (published version) + author PDF (working paper)
read_depth: full text, results sections, not cover-to-cover (Sections 1, 3.4, 5.1-5.2)
question: Did Sandy change official property assessments and tax burdens for inundated homes and for undamaged homes in high-risk zones?
data: NYC Department of Finance assessment rolls and property sales, Class 1 residential
identification: DiD inundated vs non-inundated; Zone A x post for non-inundated homes
main_finding: Inundated: sale price -10%, assessor market value -17% (mostly tax relief), assessed value -10%, taxable value -6.5% (Table 3, pp. 22-23). Non-inundated Zone A: sale price -11% but no change in assessor market, assessed or taxable values (Table 4, p. 24). Assessment caps (6%/yr, 20%/5 yrs) blunt transmission.
how_my_project_differs: Counter-example to 'no study of official values'; project studies official appraisals that anchor bank collateral (Thai Treasury), ex-ante satellite hazard, in an emerging market

authors: Hino, Burke
title: The effect of information about climate risk on property values
question: Do US housing markets price flood-zone information?
data: CoreLogic deeds for all US states 1996-2017; FEMA historical (Q3) and current flood maps; compendia of map changes
identification: Panel (same house rezoned into floodplain), DiD on small areas, and cross-section for comparison; heterogeneity by buyer type and state disclosure law
main_finding: Preferred panel estimate of the flood-zone discount is -2.1% (95% CI -4.9% to 0.8%), below the roughly -6.9% implied by insurance costs at a 5% discount rate; larger penalty for commercial buyers and in strict-disclosure states; floodplain homes overvalued by about $34bn in aggregate (WP figure).
how_my_project_differs: Map-revision design on transaction prices in the US. My project would exploit Thai hazard-map or flood-extent information as the shock and use appraisal values in a market without mandatory insurance.

authors: Kanz, Martin
title: What Does Debt Relief Do for Development? Evidence from India's Bailout for Rural Households
question: Does debt relief relax debt overhang and raise investment and productivity?

identification: RD at 2-hectare pledged-land eligibility cutoff (100% vs 25% conditional relief)
main_finding: Debt falls persistently but investment and productivity do not rise; full-relief households borrow 6 pp less from formal sources and shift to informal credit; works through expectations about future access to credit
how_my_project_differs: Relief not tied to a disaster; the project studies relief interacting with physical damage to collateral

authors: Keys, Mulder
title: Neglected No More: Housing Markets, Mortgage Lending, and Sea Level Rise
question: How have housing and mortgage markets in coastal Florida responded to sea-level-rise exposure over time?
data: Home transactions (cash and mortgaged), mortgage applications and flood insurance linked to SLR projections at census-tract level, coastal Florida, 2001-2020 (771 tracts within half a mile of the coast)
identification: Matching DiD (synthetic control, nearest neighbour, generalised propensity score) with 2001-2012 baseline; heterogeneity by poverty and climate-concern survey
main_finding: From 2013-2018 sales volumes in the most exposed tracts fell 16-20% relative to matched tracts while prices moved in step; relative prices fell 5-10% below trend by 2020. Little change in loan denial, securitisation or refinancing; authors favour a buyer-demand explanation.
how_my_project_differs: US coastal SLR, transaction data, volumes lead prices. My project asks the parallel question for appraisal values and collateral in an emerging market, where volumes and transaction prices may be thin.

authors: Mori, Nishimura, Taniguchi
title: Flood risk information effects on land price fluctuation: Using 'Safety level map of chi-saki' (in Japanese)
venue: Reports of the City Planning Institute of Japan 14(4):276-280
question: Is detailed flood-risk information (Shiga's 2012 'chi-saki' safety map) reflected in land prices?
data: 366 sites of the official Prefectural Land Price Survey (都道府県地価調査) in Shiga, 2012 and 2014; simulated inundation depth for 1/10, 1/100 and 1/200-year rainfall

how_my_project_differs: Only study found that uses official appraised land values; descriptive, two years, one prefecture, no credit link. My project would use official appraisals with a causal design and connect them to collateral and credit risk.

authors: Schüwer, U.; Lambert, C.; Noth, F.

authors: Kim, You Suk; Lee, Donghoon; Scharlemann, Tess; Vickery, James

main_finding: Moderately to severely damaged homes were more likely to go 90 days delinquent shortly after Harvey; outside mandatory-insurance zones, greater damage raised the likelihood of modification and of 180+ days delinquency or default over two years, while inside them prepayment rose with damage (IDEAS abstract)
how_my_project_differs: US setting with mandatory flood insurance as the buffer; project studies Thailand, where insurance is thin and debt relief is the buffer, and adds collateral values, LGD and capital
